reading.body:
Resemble AI builds detection systems for AI-generated audio, video, and images, positioning itself in the trust and verification layer of synthetic media rather than creation tools.

The company's market exists because voice cloning and deepfake video calls have become fraud vectors at scale. FBI data cited in the context around this company places business email compromise losses involving AI voice at over three billion dollars in 2025, a two hundred fifty million dollar increase year over year. Detection of synthetic media is not a peripheral concern but a response to specific, quantified harm in enterprise operations.

Resemble AI's architecture choice, a world model designed to recognize physical impossibilities rather than pattern-matching alone, reflects a technical bet that detection requires reasoning about what the real world permits. The company offers deployment flexibility, on-premises or cloud, which matters for customers with data sensitivity around the media they need analyzed. Neither product launch velocity, customer count, nor financial performance is covered in this data, leaving the question of detection accuracy and adoption rate unresolved.

profile_text.body:
Resemble AI is a Toronto-based company founded in 2018. Its site presents it as a provider of multimodal deepfake detection and watermarking for enterprise customers, offering real-time detection of AI-generated audio, video, and images with what it describes as explainable results. It says deployments can be on-premises or in the cloud, and describes its DETECT-World model as combining pattern matching and training with a world model architecture that recognizes deviations from physical reality.

The company also works in voice cloning, tracked as a voice and audio product and noted for likeness and consent risk. Its site frames the business as bridging AI creation tools and the trust needed to use them, and says it won the T Challenge competition run by T-Mobile US and Deutsche Telekom in 2025. A quotation carried on the site credits its speed and says it tracks where deepfake detection is heading.

Material on the site also collects reports of deepfake misuse, including an FBI figure cited by Forbes that business email compromise scams stole over $3 billion in 2025, a 2024 case at Arup where an employee wired $25.6 million after a deepfake video call, and a Hong Kong man who lost HK$10 million (US$1.27 million) in a WhatsApp scam that used AI-generated voice notes.
